source.title: RouterInterp: Understanding Superposed Specialisation in Mixture of Experts Routing
source.authors: I. Lasy; Nora Yinuo Cai; K. Ayonrinde

page_placements.theme: Attention heads and MoE experts are polysemantic at the unit level

record.tranche_reason: The study measures semantic diversity in MoE expert routing, not polysemanticity of individual neurons. Its expert-level results are related to the claim but do not test any listed neuron-focused version.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results about MoE experts and their routing, a related but different construct from individual neuron responses. Those results are recorded as findings for none of the versions. It does not measure neuron activation patterns, neuron-level capacity pressure, or whether the cited Inception neuron has a shared feature. Explanation-score comparisons evaluate the authors’ interpretation method and are not results about neuron polysemanticity.
record.test_reason: The study measures how semantically diverse MoE expert routing is, an expert-level construct, not the polysemanticity of individual neurons. It invokes superposition and polysemantic neurons only as background and as an analogy. Its neuron-basis probes are sparse linear readouts of residual-stream dimensions used as a baseline for routing prediction, not tests of neuron polysemanticity. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that expert routing is highly polysemantic: experts specialise in disjoint unions of fine-grained micro-domains (the Superposed Specialisation Hypothesis), not one coherent domain. They also conclude that RouterInterp, an SAE-feature-based method, explains routing better than token-statistics and activation-based baselines (0.49 on gpt-oss-20b, 0.60 on OLMoE). The neuron-level superposition theory is cited as an analogy, not tested.
record.recipe_differences: The study's measurements concern expert routing and SAE features, not the neuron-level methods in the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Routing-prediction performance changes with the number of active SAE features retained and varies by layer. The reported semantic-cluster averages are for the deepest tested layer in each model.

fits_no_version.finding: The top-20 routing-predictive SAE latents per expert fall into a mean of 11.3 clusters (gpt-oss-20b, layer 20) and 10.8 (OLMoE, layer 15). This is far above the 1 predicted by the DSH and below the roughly 16.6 expected from random assignment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MoE experts in the tested models route semantically heterogeneous collections of micro-domains (expert-level polysemanticity).

fits_no_version.finding: In gpt-oss-20b, routing-prediction macro-F1 generally rises with the number of active SAE features kept per token. It is not strictly monotonic: layer 4 peaks at m=64, and layer 16 dips at m=64.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MoE routing decisions depend on many SAE features jointly.

fits_no_version.finding: Expert routing preferences over Pile subsets are tightly concentrated near the corpus rate in gpt-oss-20b layers 4, 12 and 20. Some individual experts show spikes on particular subsets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Coarse dataset-source domains do not map onto dedicated MoE experts.

record.problems: The paper's main related finding relies on SAE-derived feature explanations and semantic clustering rather than direct causal tests of expert specialization. The authors note that high cluster counts could reflect inefficient or inexplicable routing; their argument against these possibilities relies on model performance and interpretable RouterInterp descriptions. The study covers two models and limited layers. The Pile-subset result is described qualitatively from a figure, without tabulated values. Human evaluation is small-scale: 150 examples across 25 experts from one layer.

untested.parts: No image classifiers or InceptionV1 neurons are studied.
No count of polysemantic MLP neurons in transformer language models; the units studied are MoE experts and SAE latents.
Superposition is used only as an analogy for expert routing. There is no test of whether neuron polysemanticity stems from more features than neurons.
Initialization, regularization and training noise are not studied at the neuron level.
No comparison of neuron polysemanticity across activation functions, architectures or regularization.
No re-examination of canonical polysemantic neurons.
No comparison of neuron polysemanticity judgments across activation ranges or scoring methods. The scorer design concerns explanations of experts, not neurons.

record.verdict_notes: The neuron-basis probe results (Tables 2 and 3) are baseline comparisons for the study's own method on residual-stream dimensions and do not bear on MLP neuron polysemanticity. They are correctly left out. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test image-classifier neurons or InceptionV1.
It studies MoE expert routing in language models, not the share of transformer MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts.

The paper discusses superposition as an analogy and proposes superposed specialisation of experts, but does not test whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by representing more features than neurons.
It does not test neuron polysemanticity under initialization, regularization, or training noise, or whether it arises without capacity pressure.
It does not measure neuron polysemanticity across activation functions, architectures, or regularization choices, nor its effect on performance.
It does not investigate whether apparently polysemantic neurons have a shared feature or whether neuron-level unrelated mixtures are rare.
It does not compare neuron-polysemanticity judgments across activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

rows.subject: gpt-oss-20b
rows.operation_detail: Cluster the explanations of each expert's top 20 predictive SAE latents by semantic similarity.
rows.measure: Mean number of distinct semantic clusters per expert (G)
rows.note: The paper reports the mean across experts; it says this is below the random-clustering expectation and far above the DSH prediction.
rows.check: Expert-level semantic diversity, not neuron-level, so it bears on no version. The baseline should also note the paper's random-clustering expectation of about 16.6 clusters; the observed 11.3 is below it.

relation.reason: Polysemantic neurons and superposition are invoked as background (Section 2.1) and as an analogy for experts (Sections 1, 3, 3.2). Nothing measures neuron-level polysemanticity.

tranche.reason: The measure is expert-level semantic diversity of routing-predictive SAE latents, not neuron polysemanticity. The residual-stream neuron-basis probes are only a routing-prediction baseline. Neurons appear only as background and analogy.

source_check.notes: Both rows and the statement match the text. Footnote 10 gives the random-assignment reference of about 16.6, and the text says observed G is slightly below it. K is about 50, chosen by silhouette (footnote 8). The rows measure experts, not neurons, so they bear on no version.

statements.correction: Mean G = 11.3 (gpt-oss-20b, layer 20) and 10.8 (OLMoE-1B-7B, layer 15), with top n=20 predictive SAE latents per expert. The DSH predicts G=1. Random assignment gives about 16.6 (20 latents among 50 equal-sized clusters; footnote 10).
